events.summary: The opener, a Go team lead, proposes making `:=` for-loop variables per-iteration instead of per-loop, gated on the go.mod go version so existing code keeps old behaviour; cites Google codebase data (about 1 in 8,000 package tests broke, almost always buggy tests), a GOEXPERIMENT=loopvar compiler mode, a bisect tool, and pre-proposal discussion #56010.
A contributor says the go.mod gating handles the compatibility concern and calls this the single real pitfall of Go, urging adoption.
A contributor notes the new semantics should apply to go 1.22 and any later version line.

A contributor strongly opposes applying the change to three-clause for loops, arguing the desugaring is too implicit and contradicts intuition that one declaration yields one variable, while supporting it for range loops.
A contributor points out the previous commenter misquoted the design doc's expansion.
The previous commenter says the expansion has been corrected and the objection stands.
A contributor shows the current expansion for comparison, arguing the proposal adds only a copy in and copy out per iteration.
The three-clause critic acknowledges the small mistake but keeps the objection.
A user supports the proposal but asks whether modifying the loop variable inside a three-clause loop body still affects later iterations.
The three-clause critic answers that the example behaves the same, but other use cases do change.
A contributor sees no argument that distinguishes three-clause loops from range loops, and says differing semantics between them would confuse.
The user replies that JavaScript and Python print 0, 2, 4 for such loops and Go would be unusual otherwise.
A contributor explains the transformed code carries the final value forward to the next iteration, so the example still prints 0, 2, 4 and only capture by address or closure changes.
The opener confirms the example is unaffected, likens the new semantics to JavaScript let, points to the design doc, and invites people to test with gotip and GOEXPERIMENT=loopvar.

The opener argues three-clause loops must change too, otherwise the hazard remains when converting between loop forms; he cites real repository fixes and Google test failures in which no correct three-clause loop broke, and asks critics for real-world counterexamples.
The user who raised the three-clause question says he misunderstood and now fully supports the proposal.
A user calls the capture problem a safety concern and urges adopting the fix quickly.
A user supports the change but worries that tools like dependabot auto-bump the go line, so a minor go.mod edit could change behaviour; asks what mental model reviewers should hold.
The opener replies that a go line bump should be treated like any dependency upgrade that is intended to be compatible but must be tested, and notes GODEBUG settings will also key on the go line.
The opener, for the proposal review group, moves the proposal into the active column for weekly review.

The three-clause critic restates support for changing range loops only, argues three-clause semantics become counter-intuitive, and offers two contrived examples whose behaviour or copying cost would change.
A contributor says the critic's examples are so contrived they say nothing about intuition and should not exist in real code.
A contributor rejects the claim the proposal is rushed, citing the prior discussion and experiment-flag issue, and notes about 230 thumbs up versus 6 thumbs down in two days.

The opener says the decision will rest on evidence, not feelings: millions of lines at Google ran the new semantics with zero three-clause breakages, and asks the critic to stop repeating arguments without real examples.
A user supports the change but fears codebases without good tests will stay on old go versions forever, and asks for an official opt-in tool that rewrites suspicious loops to keep the old behaviour.
A user argues the JavaScript comparison is misleading because var is function-scoped, and says the change is a surprising macro not worth saving one line.
A contributor replies that JavaScript let matches the proposal and var is unrepresentative.
The same user maintains the JavaScript comparison is out of place since JavaScript lacks Go-style pointers.
A contributor shows a goroutine example without pointers that prints 3, 3, 3, arguing pointers are not the crux.
The user says the contributor ignored his point that JavaScript added lexical scoping on top of var.
The contributor answers that earlier comparisons referred only to for-let, so var is irrelevant.
The user repeats that Go already has lexical scoping, so the JavaScript change is not analogous.
A contributor explains he wants the change because today a closure passed to a helper must finish before the next iteration, which makes adding t.Parallel across a large codebase hard to do safely.
A contributor says the JavaScript comparison is only explanatory, the empirical point is that people expect per-iteration variables, and range loops already carry a hidden iterator.
A user backs the range change but finds three-clause per-iteration semantics confusing, citing Stack Overflow questions about JavaScript and Dart and C#'s choice to change only foreach.
A user replies the change makes loops more intuitive and is unlikely to affect running code.
A contributor argues that whatever assumption makes real code correct is the intuitive one, and asks for a realistic example where three-clause loops become harder to read.
The user gives a closure example he would still want an explicit copy for, and says the implicit copy-back adds mental overhead absent from range loops.
A contributor says range loops already involve such an implicit copy.
The user disputes that range loops copy anything back.
The contributor says both forms use a hidden iteration variable and the added cognitive load is not credible.
The opener tells the upgrade-worried user the team will consider providing a rewrite tool that preserves old semantics as a backstop, though he would not recommend it generally.
The opener says the cited Stack Overflow posts show curiosity, not complaints, and repeats that the three-clause question will be settled by real-world data, not intuition.
The three-clause critic posts a third example in which a counter captured in a deferred closure behaves differently under the experiment.
A contributor says a behaviour difference is not a footgun.
The critic says in this thread a footgun means a surprise.
The contributor says the example behaves exactly as he would expect.
A user says the example likely reflects a bug and the new semantics still make sense.
The opener tells the critic only real code broken by the change will influence the decision and asks him to stop posting hypothetical examples.
A user asks whether a per-loop compiler directive opting out of the fix could be offered instead of a rewrite tool.
A contributor notes a per-file build constraint naming an older Go version will act as an opt-out, and says he would write the critic's counter example differently and expect it to work.
The user accepts per-file build tags as forgiving enough and doubts a rewrite tool is better.
The three-clause critic says each of his examples is distinct, argues too few Go programmers know about the change, and asks to wait for wider experiment participation before deciding.
A user replies that the question of which value is captured remains and that the opener wants people to test their own code.
A contributor reports his modules pass their tests under GOEXPERIMENT=loopvar, has no concerns, and suggests others try it, while noting his mental model of three-clause loops must change.

A user supports the range change but opposes the three-clause change, arguing the evidence is biased toward finding fixed bugs, comes only from public and Google code, and that three-clause loops allow far more varied use; he offers an example pattern he believes breaks.
A user asks whether that pattern really breaks.
A contributor says there is evidence of no three-clause breakage, not merely no evidence, and cannot see how the example breaks.
The user insists the evidence is biased and initially claims a value-returning constructor breaks, a claim he later strikes through.
A contributor runs the proposed counterexample under GOEXPERIMENT=loopvar and shows it behaves the same.
A user shows a closer emulation of the new semantics that also prints once.
A contributor says opponents offer only hypothetical code while real bugs would be fixed, and asks for evidence of bias.
The user thanks the correction but says nobody has addressed his argument that the evidence is biased.
A contributor says he did respond and invites better evidence.
A contributor argues AST tools could search for breakages, that bugs in Google and public code show people think alike, and that objections rest only on what might happen.
The three-clause critic says the onus to find real-world breakages lies with the proposers, not him.
The critic proposes an alternative: allow a redeclaration in the third clause so per-iteration scoping is explicit, possibly applied by go fix.
A user notes synthetic examples are easy and only real code relying on the old rules would be convincing.
A contributor says a single real example would not overturn the evidence unless it showed a common pattern or a novel natural mistake.
The critic repeats that proving no breakage is the proposers' job.
A user says the request is for people to report cases from their own code, a distributed effort.
A contributor says the claim was never zero breakage but far more fixes than breaks, and suggests disengaging from demands to prove a negative.

The user argues breaking the stability promise needs near-zero breakage, which he grants for range loops but not three-clause loops, calls for wider sampling such as an industry survey, and suggests a Go 2 would make such a change clearer.
The opener tells the two three-clause critics their arguments have been heard and understood, and asks them to make room for other concerns.
The bias critic says his challenge to the evidence went unanswered but agrees to step back, and asks that any release prominently announce the semantic change.
A user welcomes the change and asks to see the one non-test breakage found at Google and any other known breakages.
A maintainer points to the design doc section describing that case, an allocation-free low-level crash handler.
The user thanks him and asks to hear of any other breakages.
The three-clause critic points the user to his earlier hypothetical examples.
The co-author explains the one failure involved taking an address on a path ending in break, and a pickier compiler analysis could have avoided the extra allocation there.
A maintainer asks the co-author to confirm that a future compiler optimisation could have avoided the allocation that test forbade.
A user, initially bothered by the small performance cost, says he will favour index loops for slices and sees the change as welcoming to newcomers.
The co-author confirms that a trickier optimisation would have avoided that one failure.
A user says he hit this bug only once or twice in five years and questions whether the cure is worth the cognitive cost of checking each module's go version.
The three-clause critic agrees that version numbers should not mark behaviour changes.
A user objects that the change breaks the Go 1 compatibility promise and fears subtle bugs in upgraded third-party dependencies.
A contributor argues small individual rates add up across about a million developers, the bisect tool narrows which loops to check, and per-file build tags offer an escape hatch.
A contributor says the proposal knowingly makes a one-time exception to compatibility, and dependencies keep old semantics until their own go.mod is bumped.
A maintainer gives non-concurrency examples, including an x/crypto/ssh bug fixed in a CL, that long-time contributors failed to spot and the race detector cannot catch.
A user argues the fix could mask later bugs because a pointer to the per-iteration copy will not update the slice, and suggests ranging over element addresses instead.
A contributor says the user's examples behave identically before and after the proposal.
A user agrees the pointer never pointed into the slice and says go.mod gating confines changes to upgraded code.
A maintainer shows how to try the experiment with gotip and runs the user's example: the new semantics fix the first print and leave the slice unchanged in both versions.
A contributor notes Go has broken compatibility before for correctness reasons.
The compatibility objector replies those earlier changes produced compile errors, unlike this silent behaviour change.
A user argues the change is not silent since a version number must be bumped.
The objector says upgrades are eventually forced as old versions lose support, so the risk remains.
The pointer-concern user explains the new semantics could make code that only reads the copy appear correct, hiding a later write that fails to reach the slice.
A contributor points the pointer-concern user to a related issue and a comment in the earlier discussion.
A contributor argues languages must fix old mistakes rather than pile up alternative forms as C++ did.

A contributor calls the pointer scenario a thin chain of misunderstandings, and lays out that the proposal does break the compatibility promise and the Go 2 transition rules, which the proposal openly treats as a one-time exception that sets no precedent.
The pointer-concern user concedes the argument is narrow, says he is not against the proposal, and asks whether the authors have more motivating context than one parallel example.
A contributor says reaction on the issue, the earlier discussion and social media has been overwhelmingly positive, so the fix is not academic.
The three-clause critic asks whether the vote on his first comment counts as overwhelming and says some breaking cases are missing from the proposal.
A contributor contrasts that with the opening post's tally and tells the critic his synthetic examples have been addressed and he should stop.
The opener thanks the helpers and cites the Let's Encrypt incident, where a carefully reviewed loop still captured a variable and led to a mass certificate revocation question, as proof of real harm.

A maintainer notes the critic's comment drew more downvotes than upvotes during early confusion, says emoji votes are only a rough measure, and expects the Go 1.21 experiment to surface any real impact.

The opener reports running Kubernetes tests with the experiment: two loopvar failures in about 1,054 packages, both test bugs pinpointed by the bisect tool, versus 1 in 8,000 at Google; go-ethereum had no failures.
A contributor asks the critic to stop arguing over vote wording and says production evidence like Kubernetes is more useful than his examples.

The pointer-concern user is now convinced the bug is real but asks why promoting the loopclosure vet check, or adding a pointer-taking check, would not suffice; he later finds the design doc addresses static analysis.
A user points to the design doc section rejecting static analysis as an alternative.
A contributor adds that even with vet the remedy is a confusing redundant copy line.
The same user regrets that the post statement now effectively acts on a copied variable, making loops less explicit.
A contributor finds that loop easy to read and asks the discussion to stop going in circles.
A contributor says behaviour is unchanged unless pointers or closures are involved and suggests some objections stem only from resistance to change.
The user accepts this and withdraws.

The three-clause critic posts a final comment arguing the opening post understated the three-clause change, that version-gated semantics are a bad idea, and that the change reduces loop flexibility; he leaves the debate.
A user says the change adds needless complexity and undermines compatibility.
A user endorses controlled change tied to the compiler version.
A bot links a change documenting GOEXPERIMENT=loopvar in the Go 1.21 release notes and inviting feedback.
A contributor from Let's Encrypt says they enabled the experiment in CI with no breakages or newly revealed bugs and welcome the change.

The opener says response has been overwhelmingly positive and two large codebases ran the always-on experiment without trouble, so the proposal will move to likely accept to land early in Go 1.22, still open to showstoppers.
The opener, for the proposal review group, marks the proposal likely accept.
The opener applies the final comment period label.
The opener, for the proposal review group, declares the proposal accepted with no change in consensus, and says the issue now tracks implementation.
The opener drops the proposal prefix from the title.
The opener applies the Proposal-Accepted label.
The opener removes the final comment period label.
A user worries this is a semantic-only change that will not fail visibly on older toolchains, then notes the design doc addresses it as a one-time exception.
A contributor confirms it is the first such change and is meant to be the last.
The opener says the Go playground now supports trying the new semantics with a GOEXPERIMENT comment on Go 1.21.
A bot links a change making the Go 1.20 toolchain refuse to build Go 1.22 code.
A bot links the same refusal change for the Go 1.19 branch.

A user, after acceptance, backs the three-clause critic, arguing that other languages' loops mostly keep one variable and that the proposal should have been split so three-clause loops got a separate vote.
A user says he always assumed loop variables were closure-safe and supports going ahead.
A bot links a change updating go/ssa for the new range variable semantics.
A user worries about unnoticed breakage in untested range loops and suggests a new keyword or a migration tool that preserves old behaviour.
A contributor explains a new keyword would break compatibility and the design doc covers why syntax changes and migration rewriting were rejected.
A contributor says large codebases like Kubernetes showed no problems and the argument adds nothing new.
A Go team member points to the design doc's transition tooling section as the basis for such a migration tool.
A user suggests closures could capture values rather than references, as some Lisps do, as a more general alternative.
A maintainer proposes closing the issue as done now that Go 1.22 has shipped.
A maintainer closes the issue as completed.
A comment GitHub marks as hidden (off-topic).
The issue is locked.
